title: {{NAME}} and the Match at the End of the World
moral: The best teams are built on trust, not just talent.

pages.content: The stadium at the top of Copper Hill was unlike any place {{NAME}} had ever seen. Its arching walls were grown from living vines, threaded with glowing amber circuits that pulsed like a slow heartbeat. The pitch itself was a carpet of the greenest grass imaginable, so vivid it almost hummed. In the centre circle stood a robot the size of a large labrador, built from burnished copper plates and fitted with enormous springy legs. It was juggling a soccer ball on its head with mathematical perfection. Around the pitch, animals filled the terraced seats, cheering and stamping: badgers in scarves, otters waving pennants, a row of rabbits sharing a single enormous bag of seeds. {{NAME}} had been invited here by a talking fox named Cleo, who sat beside him now in the dugout, clipboard in paw. 'The Ironpaws need a striker,' she said crisply. 'Their last one sprained an ankle chasing a butterfly.' {{NAME}} looked at the copper robot on the pitch and swallowed.

pages.content: The copper robot rolled across the pitch and extended a hand that was also, somehow, a very precise compass. 'I am BOLT-7,' it said, its voice a warm, rattling baritone like pebbles in a tin drum. 'I calculate the optimal trajectory of every pass. I have never missed a cross.' It stared at {{NAME}} with round lenses that whirred as they focused. 'Your feet are smaller than projected. Recalibrating.' {{NAME}} laughed, which seemed to confuse BOLT-7 considerably. The robot tilted its copper head, gears clicking. 'Why do you make that noise?' it asked. 'Because you said something funny,' said {{NAME}}. 'My data shows no joke was made,' BOLT-7 replied, entirely seriously. Cleo the fox snorted behind her clipboard. The other animal players emerged from the tunnel then, a mongoose named Dash, quick as a struck match, and a broad-shouldered bear cub called Remy, solid as a doorstep. They were a good team, {{NAME}} could see that immediately. But they did not yet trust each other.

pages.content: The match began at sunset, the sky bruising purple and orange above the vine-walls, and the opposing team, the Rustclaw Badgers, proved ferocious. They were fast, low to the ground, and had a goalkeeper made entirely of interlocking metal plates who deflected shots with its whole body like a living wall. Dash the mongoose darted through three defenders in a single breath, but his shot went wide. Remy the bear thundered forward but passed too late. BOLT-7 computed the perfect cross but executed it so mechanically that every player expected it and the Badgers stepped in. Nil-nil at half time. In the dugout, Cleo paced. {{NAME}} sat thinking, bouncing the ball on his knee. The problem was not skill. Each player had more skill than they needed. The problem was that they each played as if the others did not exist. He stood up. 'BOLT-7,' he said, 'stop calculating the perfect pass. Just watch Dash and pass when his eyes light up.' The robot's lenses whirred. 'Insufficient data,' it said. 'Trust me,' said {{NAME}}. 'I have analysed trust,' said BOLT-7. 'It has a 73% failure rate.' 'And a 100% chance of being worth it,' said {{NAME}}.

pages.content: The second half was a different game entirely. BOLT-7 stopped computing and started watching. Dash blazed down the right flank, his eyes bright with concentration, and the moment his head angled forward, BOLT-7 swung its springy leg and the ball arrived at exactly the right place at exactly the right moment, not because of maths but because of attention. Dash struck it perfectly. The metal goalkeeper flung itself sideways. The ball curved over its outstretched arm and hit the back of the net with a sound like a bell. The animals in the stands erupted. Badgers howled. Otters slapped the railings. The rabbits sent their enormous bag of seeds flying in every direction. Remy the bear lifted {{NAME}} off the ground in a hug so exuberant that the world went briefly upside down. Even BOLT-7, who insisted it did not experience joy, was spinning slowly in a small circle, its copper plates glowing a warm, unmistakeable gold.

pages.content: After the final whistle, when the amber circuit-lights in the vine-walls had dimmed to a drowsy gold, {{NAME}} sat on the pitch with Dash, Remy, and BOLT-7, eating oranges that Cleo had produced from somewhere mysterious inside her vest. The grass was cool and damp. The stars above the open stadium were sharp and thick as scattered sugar. BOLT-7 peeled its orange with geometric precision, separating each segment to exactly the same size. 'I am recalibrating my trust data,' it announced. 'New sample size: one.' Remy laughed, low and rolling, and Dash flicked an orange pip at the robot's copper nose. {{NAME}} leaned back on his hands, full of warmth and orange juice and the good ache of a hard match well played. Cleo appeared at his shoulder. 'Get some sleep,' she said, in that crisp fox way of hers. 'Training is at dawn.' {{NAME}} closed his eyes and smiled. He wondered, just before sleep took him, whether BOLT-7 ever dreamed, and if so, what a robot's dream of a perfect game might look like.
